summary: Oxyphenonium bromide is a quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) agent used as a gastrointestinal antispasmodic and, historically, as adjunctive therapy for peptic ulcer disease to reduce gastric motility and secretion. As a quaternary compound it penetrates the central nervous system poorly. It is not an FDA-approved drug in the United States and is used under EMA/national labeling. Typical adverse effects are anticholinergic: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, and urinary retention. It is contraindicated in glaucoma, urinary retention, and obstructive GI disease.

Adjunctive treatment of peptic ulcer disease (historical) to reduce gastric motility and secretion

moa: Oxyphenonium bromide is a synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinic agent that competitively and reversibly antagonizes acetylcholine at muscarinic (parasympathetic) receptors on smooth muscle, secretory glands, and cardiac tissue. In the gastrointestinal tract this reduces smooth muscle tone and peristalsis (antispasmodic effect) and decreases gastric acid and other glandular secretions (antisecretory effect). Because it is a charged quaternary compound, it crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, limiting central effects compared with tertiary amine anticholinergics.

absolute: Urinary retention or significant bladder outflow obstruction (e.g., prostatic hypertrophy)
Gastrointestinal obstruction, paralytic ileus, or severe ulcerative colitis/toxic megacolon
relative: Coronary artery disease, tachyarrhythmia, or heart failure

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. Use only if clearly needed and the potential benefit justifies the potential risk; prefer non-anticholinergic alternatives where possible.
lact: Anticholinergic agents may reduce milk production and small amounts may pass into breast milk. Use with caution during breastfeeding and monitor the infant for anticholinergic effects.
renal: Specific data are limited; use with caution in renal impairment as a quaternary ammonium compound is partly renally eliminated.
hepatic: Specific data are limited; use with caution in hepatic impairment.

moderate: Other anticholinergic drugs (antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiparkinson agents) - additive anticholinergic toxicity
Potassium chloride (solid oral forms) - delayed GI transit increases mucosal injury risk
Drugs whose absorption depends on GI motility (e.g., levodopa, ketoconazole) - altered absorption
minor: Antacids/adsorbents - may reduce absorption; separate administration
Metoclopramide - opposing effects on GI motility

counsel: Take this medicine before meals as directed for stomach cramps or spasm
Dry mouth, blurred vision, and constipation are common - sip water, use sugar-free gum, and eat fiber
Be careful in hot weather and during exercise, as this medicine reduces sweating and can cause overheating
Tell your doctor if you have trouble passing urine, eye pain, or sudden vision changes
Avoid driving until you know how blurred vision or dizziness affects you
pk: Plasma effect within 1-2 hours (limited published data)
Short; effects typically last a few hours requiring multiple daily doses
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the United States; used under EMA/national labeling - dosing reflects those sources, not an FDA label
Quaternary ammonium structure limits CNS penetration, so central anticholinergic effects are less prominent than with tertiary amines
Classic contraindications: angle-closure glaucoma, urinary obstruction, GI obstruction, myasthenia gravis
Largely superseded by selective antisecretory agents (H2 blockers, PPIs) and modern antispasmodics
Caution in the elderly and in hot environments due to anticholinergic burden and impaired sweating
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Overdose produces an anticholinergic toxidrome: dry flushed skin, dilated pupils, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention, hyperthermia, agitation, and in severe cases delirium, seizures, or circulatory failure. Management is supportive; physostigmine may be considered for severe central anticholinergic toxicity under specialist guidance. Contact a poison control center.
